d22c263c-f45f-4b8c-a442-0fc09640467b.definition: Ability to deploy and evaluate typically complex systems such as Spark based on documentation.

8614a1fa-5079-46d4-88f0-b66b5931724f.title: Interactive Program Design
8614a1fa-5079-46d4-88f0-b66b5931724f.definition: Ability to design and implement a simple interactive program.

4e9e664e-7fcd-46f7-a8af-c665fc264b2c.title: Web Server Design
4e9e664e-7fcd-46f7-a8af-c665fc264b2c.definition: Ability to design and deploy a simple web server.

f3b9ef89-b40a-48d1-ab54-903392de24ba.title: Data Storage Design
f3b9ef89-b40a-48d1-ab54-903392de24ba.definition: Ability to design and implement a simple data storage system.

f1ce7a4b-b9ac-4e0b-8e42-c8b9f496a3bd.title: Advanced Computer Systems
f1ce7a4b-b9ac-4e0b-8e42-c8b9f496a3bd.definition: In-depth overview of the architecture, components, and operations of computer systems.

ba7dc8ce-b66d-4ce3-9335-081d60d18ef5.title: Advanced System Design
ba7dc8ce-b66d-4ce3-9335-081d60d18ef5.definition: Study the principles and methods of computer system design at an advanced level.

fc2b702c-f13f-4f75-975f-516b8e138db0.title: OS Purpose
fc2b702c-f13f-4f75-975f-516b8e138db0.definition: understand the purpose, function and role of the operating system in resource management and service provision.

8c2a3e0c-a3f3-458a-b79b-18f57e084d2c.title: OS Principles
8c2a3e0c-a3f3-458a-b79b-18f57e084d2c.definition: Master the fundamentals behind the design and operation of operating systems.

233823d8-7f1a-4ef8-9dbb-ccb6b3d07d4e.title: Networking Basics
233823d8-7f1a-4ef8-9dbb-ccb6b3d07d4e.definition: Basic concepts and operating principles of computer networks.

87ff6a4f-ec58-4639-ade0-41134dc72f52.title: Network Applications
87ff6a4f-ec58-4639-ade0-41134dc72f52.definition: Research applications built and operating on computer network platforms.

1ee86676-3cd8-4fe6-991b-6afa05affd1e.title: Parallel & Distributed Computing
1ee86676-3cd8-4fe6-991b-6afa05affd1e.definition: understand the design and implementation of programs in parallel and distributed computing environments.

b8f1dc90-6f23-4928-9b41-9669442b827f.title: Computer Arch: I/O
b8f1dc90-6f23-4928-9b41-9669442b827f.definition: Research the mechanisms and operating principles of input/output systems in computer architecture.

0ddc1139-37d4-4de4-b70d-65d8d690b689.title: Computer Arch: Perf & Power
0ddc1139-37d4-4de4-b70d-65d8d690b689.definition: analyze the relationship between performance and energy consumption in computer architecture design.

0b5c904e-9491-4055-a62e-9a9ea24cba21.title: Advanced System Reliability
0b5c904e-9491-4055-a62e-9a9ea24cba21.definition: Advanced methods and techniques to ensure computer system reliability.

11fbc9d0-9eb2-4b22-bc35-152f9c935a8c.title: Advanced System Performance
11fbc9d0-9eb2-4b22-bc35-152f9c935a8c.definition: Advanced techniques and models to optimize the performance of computer systems.

0aba1426-c4f9-4390-8946-994d8e623597.title: Advanced System Security
0aba1426-c4f9-4390-8946-994d8e623597.definition: In-depth topics in computer system security, including advanced threats and prevention measures.

73edc6d1-ef0d-447e-a712-b19c0a6dc79f.title: Advanced Systems Engineering
73edc6d1-ef0d-447e-a712-b19c0a6dc79f.definition: Systems engineering processes and methods at an advanced level.

f917f99f-b0d4-4c1a-90c2-3d94093785e6.title: Queueing Theory Basics
f917f99f-b0d4-4c1a-90c2-3d94093785e6.definition: understand basic models and applications of queuing theory.

51243795-6e05-4f7b-8063-eb601ee43576.title: Random Processes
51243795-6e05-4f7b-8063-eb601ee43576.definition: understand the concepts and classifications of stochastic processes.

e25d35d6-c923-4c18-bf23-f97766211eaf.title: Linux System Design
e25d35d6-c923-4c18-bf23-f97766211eaf.definition: analyze the design principles applied in the Linux operating system.

9ff706cf-9668-4100-973a-897bb45ef7bf.title: SQL System Design
9ff706cf-9668-4100-973a-897bb45ef7bf.definition: analyze the design principles applied in SQL database systems.

1522707d-48e6-40c2-977f-6772a3d0b822.title: TCP/IP Stack Design
1522707d-48e6-40c2-977f-6772a3d0b822.definition: analyze the design principles applied in the TCP/IP network protocol stack.

7dd1a80b-b6b0-49dd-a0ef-66490195168d.title: Hadoop System Design
7dd1a80b-b6b0-49dd-a0ef-66490195168d.definition: analyze the design principles applied in the Hadoop system.

d33f0758-7963-4b9f-9eae-bfdb91180af7.title: Spark System Design
d33f0758-7963-4b9f-9eae-bfdb91180af7.definition: analyze the design principles applied in the Spark system at an advanced level.

1827f093-8ae8-4254-8ef6-f0b01677883e.title: Distributed Storage Design
1827f093-8ae8-4254-8ef6-f0b01677883e.definition: analyze design principles applied in distributed storage systems.

c3f64b5c-af7b-4d3c-a19c-6bd6a3694a76.title: File System Design
c3f64b5c-af7b-4d3c-a19c-6bd6a3694a76.definition: Ability to design and implement a complex file system.

3331814c-b593-420a-8de6-3aff6b5c7e61.title: High-Perf Web Server Design
3331814c-b593-420a-8de6-3aff6b5c7e61.definition: Ability to design and deploy a high-performance web server.

29b31519-9ddb-4d4b-82b7-e34d20328a6b.title: Specialized Platform Dev (SPD)
29b31519-9ddb-4d4b-82b7-e34d20328a6b.definition: The Specialized Platform Development (SPD) knowledge area deals with properties that include the creation of software targeting non-traditional hardware platforms. Social and industrial demands have created a high demand for developers on specialized platforms. This is an area where there has been an increase in required hours of study in CS Core compared to CS2013, reflecting the increasing deployment of specialized hardware platforms.

2d5b789b-5255-4410-847e-dfb1ae99364d.title: Non-Traditional HW Dev
2d5b789b-5255-4410-847e-dfb1ae99364d.definition: The core concept of SPD, which refers to creating software specifically designed for types of hardware other than traditional desktops or servers, requires unique considerations during development.

e612972d-13c7-4aab-bbe9-65fb4d7e2f95.title: Robotics Platforms
e612972d-13c7-4aab-bbe9-65fb4d7e2f95.definition: Develop software and applications for robotic systems, including unique considerations and challenges related to robotic hardware, sensors, actuators, and interactions with the physical environment. This is an important unit of knowledge in SPD.

ee909031-52be-471c-8b51-9dcaddb0e402.title: Mobile Systems & Apps
ee909031-52be-471c-8b51-9dcaddb0e402.definition: Develop software and applications for mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets, including elements such as touchscreens, device sensors, power management and cross-platform compatibility. This is an example of a specialized platform.

4a971798-9f86-4429-aaad-24dd1be498f4.title: Web Systems & Platforms
4a971798-9f86-4429-aaad-24dd1be498f4.definition: Develop web-based applications and services, including client-server architecture, web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), scalability and security. This is an example of a specialized platform.

8eb3eb41-e61a-4bb4-b2fe-f11df4f354b3.title: Embedded Systems
8eb3eb41-e61a-4bb4-b2fe-f11df4f354b3.definition: Software development for specialized computer systems embedded in larger devices or systems, often with limited resources and real-time requirements. This is an important unit of knowledge in SPD.

45611d57-f0b0-4c50-9f56-bc2e1fde1381.title: Multi-Device UX
45611d57-f0b0-4c50-9f56-bc2e1fde1381.definition: The ability to design and deploy applications that provide a seamless and consistent user experience regardless of the device, screen size, or operating system the user is using. This is one of the unique professional capabilities in the SPD field.

b406865c-5c16-414a-ac57-83aff7ecdf1a.title: Specialized Platform API Dev
b406865c-5c16-414a-ac57-83aff7ecdf1a.definition: Skills to create application programming interfaces (APIs) to enable software components to interact with each other and with hardware, supporting the specific and unique functions of each specialized platform. This is one of the unique professional capabilities in the SPD field.

fd5caaf0-eae9-41c9-87f0-e9bc17643263.title: Resource Constraint Management
fd5caaf0-eae9-41c9-87f0-e9bc17643263.definition: Ability to cope with and optimize the use of limited resources such as computing power, memory capacity, storage space, and network/communication bandwidth. Effective management of these limits is critical in development for specialized platforms. This is one of the unique professional capabilities in the SPD field.

9a3409b3-52d4-41ba-82ae-86eba1a741fc.title: Cross-Cutting Concerns
9a3409b3-52d4-41ba-82ae-86eba1a741fc.definition: Skill in applying critical and cross-cutting aspects of the software development process, including optimizing performance, ensuring system security, and adhering to best software development practices to improve quality and efficiency. This is one of the unique professional capabilities in the SPD field.

7ae7c8dc-d107-4221-9255-ffef64f4a9c6.title: Network Address Translation (NAT)
7ae7c8dc-d107-4221-9255-ffef64f4a9c6.definition: A fundamental networking technique that modifies IP address and port information in packet headers while they traverse a routing device, enabling multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address. It functions by maintaining a translation table.

bb384835-c3fb-4ae8-a3df-0f0f366fbb63.title: IPv4 address space conservation
bb384835-c3fb-4ae8-a3df-0f0f366fbb63.definition: The primary benefit and reason for NAT's existence, allowing the reuse of limited IPv4 address ranges by enabling many private devices to share a single public IP, thereby conserving the available global IPv4 addresses.

b5227b6e-22f9-45c6-977c-9e41ec302b01.title: Translation table
b5227b6e-22f9-45c6-977c-9e41ec302b01.definition: A data structure maintained by a NAT device that stores mappings between private IP addresses and ports and unique public IP addresses and ports, crucial for correctly routing packets.

69726e78-c879-400d-80cc-9de5630ddb45.title: Port Address Translation (PAT)
69726e78-c879-400d-80cc-9de5630ddb45.definition: Also known as NAT Overload, this is the most common form of NAT, allowing multiple private IP addresses to share a single public IP address by uniquely assigning different port numbers to each connection.

63b1885c-0df2-467b-a0ee-7a6ea9b3c2c2.title: Static NAT
63b1885c-0df2-467b-a0ee-7a6ea9b3c2c2.definition: A specific type of Network Address Translation that establishes a fixed, one-to-one mapping between a single private IP address and a single public IP address.

67a90057-cf15-4e33-8326-45cfd8001dea.title: Dynamic NAT
67a90057-cf15-4e33-8326-45cfd8001dea.definition: A type of Network Address Translation that maps a private IP address to one of a pool of available public IP addresses, typically assigned on a first-come, first-served basis.

05e1c9b9-f86c-47f1-a320-998b5aab49ad.title: End-to-end principle
05e1c9b9-f86c-47f1-a320-998b5aab49ad.definition: A fundamental networking design principle implying that intelligence should primarily reside in end hosts, which NAT breaks by modifying packet headers mid-transit and complicating certain protocols that rely on transparent end-to-end communication.

684f9912-e89f-435e-9bde-a3679be81028.title: Application-Level Gateways (ALGs)
684f9912-e89f-435e-9bde-a3679be81028.definition: Specialized network components or techniques used to address complexities introduced by NAT, particularly for protocols (like FTP, SIP) that embed IP address information within their payloads, by modifying application-level data to ensure compatibility.

f393c7aa-9319-473a-b6ce-ed68ed287e50.title: IP address
f393c7aa-9319-473a-b6ce-ed68ed287e50.definition: A unique numerical label used in networking for identifying devices, which NAT modifies in packet headers to facilitate communication between private and public networks.

32570b5e-6690-4c45-9bf9-3789faa18c69.title: Port space exhaustion
32570b5e-6690-4c45-9bf9-3789faa18c69.definition: A common operational pitfall in NAT, particularly with Port Address Translation (PAT), where the NAT device runs out of available port numbers to assign for new connections, leading to connection failures and service disruptions.

ff69f068-98ed-48c5-baa9-e5f6294ba253.title: Private network
ff69f068-98ed-48c5-baa9-e5f6294ba253.definition: A local area network that uses specific IP address ranges (e.g., 192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x) that are not directly routable on the public internet, typically residing behind a NAT device.

004e2fcf-6d8a-4c04-9131-041f67c42116.title: Public IP address
004e2fcf-6d8a-4c04-9131-041f67c42116.definition: A globally unique IP address used on the internet, which a NAT device uses to represent multiple devices from a private network when communicating with public servers.

405a1152-9842-4e72-87d5-43602b95f982.title: Rate limiting
405a1152-9842-4e72-87d5-43602b95f982.definition: A critical mechanism in distributed systems that strictly enforces a maximum request count within a time window, leading to request rejection once the limit is hit. Its primary purposes are to prevent abuse, ensure fair resource allocation, maintain system stability, and manage operational costs.

3dbba856-f6c1-4ea5-b234-df4c9f3087a3.title: Throttling
3dbba856-f6c1-4ea5-b234-df4c9f3087a3.definition: A mechanism in distributed systems that implies a more nuanced control over request rates, potentially delaying or reducing the processing priority of requests rather than outright dropping them. It's often used to manage overall resource consumption rather than just request volume.

5422683f-9117-44c9-ae32-4b68cb83a0e9.title: Fixed Window Counter
5422683f-9117-44c9-ae32-4b68cb83a0e9.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that maintains a simple counter which resets at fixed time intervals. It offers O(1) time complexity for checks and O(N) space for N clients, but is susceptible to burst traffic occurring at the boundaries of the windows.

8e7e3b44-f3eb-4823-8c60-033099e12661.title: Sliding Window Log
8e7e3b44-f3eb-4823-8c60-033099e12661.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that stores timestamps of all requests. It checks for requests within the current time window, providing high accuracy. However, it incurs O(K) time complexity per check (where K is the maximum requests in the window) and O(K) space per client.

c154c7a2-7b22-4035-918d-0543b449411f.title: Token Bucket algorithm
c154c7a2-7b22-4035-918d-0543b449411f.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that allows for a certain degree of burstiness. It refills tokens at a fixed rate up to a capacity, with each request consuming a token. It offers O(1) time and O(N) space.

4f668b9c-c55e-4f63-adc1-efbf269ec0cc.title: Leaky Bucket algorithm
4f668b9c-c55e-4f63-adc1-efbf269ec0cc.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that smooths out request bursts by processing requests from an internal queue at a steady rate. Requests are dropped if the bucket (queue) overflows. It also offers O(1) time and O(N) space plus queue overhead.

fdadedb2-a00e-4858-acdb-99d9aafb38a2.title: Sliding Window Counter
fdadedb2-a00e-4858-acdb-99d9aafb38a2.definition: A rate limiting algorithm that offers a more efficient approximation than the Sliding Window Log by combining counts from current and previous fixed windows. It achieves O(1) time and O(N) space.

b7121df5-4e0d-4038-b203-82eaff38003c.title: Distributed systems
b7121df5-4e0d-4038-b203-82eaff38003c.definition: Systems where components located on networked computers communicate and coordinate their actions by passing messages. In this context, they are the environment where rate limiting and throttling are applied to control resource access.

f822e32e-3c42-4cc3-9f85-703f8517972f.title: API gateways
f822e32e-3c42-4cc3-9f85-703f8517972f.definition: A management tool or service that acts as a single entry point for a group of microservices. They are a pervasive real-world application point for rate limiting, used to protect backend services by enforcing limits at the network edge.

21dfd457-2972-4a6d-b114-2b6788adcfac.title: Thundering herd problem
21dfd457-2972-4a6d-b114-2b6788adcfac.definition: A common pitfall in distributed systems where many processes or threads, upon being notified of an event (e.g., a service recovery), all attempt to perform an action simultaneously, often due to 'synchronized retries', leading to system overload.

b7612cd9-ee0a-4dd9-94b3-d3bb93760930.title: Geographically distributed systems
b7612cd9-ee0a-4dd9-94b3-d3bb93760930.definition: Distributed systems where components are deployed across multiple distinct physical locations. This setup introduces specific challenges for managing state consistently, especially for mechanisms like rate limiting.

a8b27efe-79dd-4921-af15-6ee1a73aeb84.title: Circuit breakers
a8b27efe-79dd-4921-af15-6ee1a73aeb84.definition: A design pattern in distributed systems to protect against cascading failures. They monitor service calls and, if failures reach a certain threshold, 'trip' to prevent further calls to the failing service, distinct from rate limiting which protects healthy services from overload.

b75133fb-a84d-4b96-b638-13f5dc48fe92.title: Message Queues
b75133fb-a84d-4b96-b638-13f5dc48fe92.definition: A fundamental component in asynchronous inter-service communication, acting as a buffer that decouples senders (producers) from receivers (consumers) by storing messages reliably until they can be processed, typically involving a broker to manage delivery.

96aa3aee-f4f8-4f1c-ab3f-9a75df4e5da2.title: Event-Driven Architecture (EDA)
96aa3aee-f4f8-4f1c-ab3f-9a75df4e5da2.definition: An architectural paradigm where services communicate by producing and consuming events representing significant state changes, often via an event broker, leading to highly decoupled, scalable, and responsive distributed systems. It offers superior fault tolerance, scalability, and loose coupling compared to synchronous models but introduces complexities like eventual consistency and message ordering.

50ab7c2a-3d25-4437-ad22-7c59c920ebda.title: Asynchronous Communication
50ab7c2a-3d25-4437-ad22-7c59c920ebda.definition: A communication model where senders do not wait for a direct response from receivers, allowing for decoupled operations, increased resilience, and parallel task execution in distributed systems.

a9003548-fa2c-449b-a498-c7adbc691f27.title: Consumer
a9003548-fa2c-449b-a498-c7adbc691f27.definition: A component or service in a message queue or event-driven system responsible for receiving or subscribing to messages or events from a broker, processing them, and acknowledging their receipt.

d90426ef-8d25-467f-860a-e44a39621f41.title: Producer
d90426ef-8d25-467f-860a-e44a39621f41.definition: A component or service in a message queue or event-driven system responsible for sending or publishing messages or events to a broker.

1a9ea8b4-9a05-472f-80fc-7201b742e971.title: Event Broker
1a9ea8b4-9a05-472f-80fc-7201b742e971.definition: A central component in message queue and event-driven systems that manages queues, stores messages or events, and facilitates their reliable delivery from producers to consumers. Examples include Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, Azure Service Bus, or Google Cloud Pub/Sub.

1ce90b6e-92c0-4f67-9aa0-dd7619b90804.title: Loose Coupling
1ce90b6e-92c0-4f67-9aa0-dd7619b90804.definition: A design principle in which components of a system have little or no direct knowledge of each other's implementation, allowing them to operate and evolve independently. This enhances flexibility, resilience, and scalability, as achieved by message queues and EDA where producers do not need to know about or wait for consumers.

2bd44203-12b8-4efd-8fe6-dfc0b2d6086d.title: Dead Letter Queues (DLQs)
2bd44203-12b8-4efd-8fe6-dfc0b2d6086d.definition: A dedicated queue used in message queue systems to store messages that could not be successfully processed after a certain number of retries or due to other processing failures, facilitating error handling and debugging.

45496eb9-aa38-4bee-b30d-2158af85e510.title: Load Leveling
45496eb9-aa38-4bee-b30d-2158af85e510.definition: A technique used in distributed systems, often implemented with message queues, to smooth out transient spikes in processing demand by buffering tasks. This ensures a more consistent workload for consumers and prevents system overload, contributing to overall system resilience.

5a9aae96-d530-4991-82ca-5529e1b0f8c3.title: Idempotency
5a9aae96-d530-4991-82ca-5529e1b0f8c3.definition: The property of an operation or a consumer service such that performing it multiple times has the same effect as performing it once, which is required in event-driven architectures for safely handling potential duplicate messages.

5a1e337e-4d5f-4249-bf0d-ff5845364678.title: Resilience / Fault Tolerance
5a1e337e-4d5f-4249-bf0d-ff5845364678.definition: The inherent ability of a system to continue operating and providing its services effectively even when components fail. This is a key benefit of message queues and event-driven architectures, often achieved through redundancy, robust error handling, and reliable message storage.

d17d13b0-45ef-4a4f-a1bf-879d4cc28d97.title: Eventual Consistency
d17d13b0-45ef-4a4f-a1bf-879d4cc28d97.definition: A characteristic of distributed systems where, after an update, all copies of the data will eventually reflect that update, though there might be a period of temporary inconsistency. Ensuring this across services is identified as a key challenge in Event-Driven Architecture.

5e61dd2e-ae5a-411d-9395-42bda1b1f52d.title: Time Complexity
5e61dd2e-ae5a-411d-9395-42bda1b1f52d.definition: A measure of the amount of time taken by an algorithm to run, expressed as a function of the input size (e.g., O(1) for simple distribution or O(log S) to O(S) for state-aware strategies, where S is the number of backend servers).

ac871ad7-d99c-48fe-b073-2fa8e0603dce.title: High Availability
ac871ad7-d99c-48fe-b073-2fa8e0603dce.definition: A system property ensuring that an application or service remains continuously operational and accessible to users, even in the event of component failures, often achieved through redundancy and failover mechanisms.

c8df3fe6-2309-426c-a7a4-1cbe4c972a46.title: Scalability
c8df3fe6-2309-426c-a7a4-1cbe4c972a46.definition: A system property referring to its ability to handle an increasing amount of work or its potential to be enlarged to accommodate that growth, often by adding resources (e.g., servers).

8391158a-d3fa-416c-9e98-ee61a2fb12f1.title: Session Persistence (Sticky Sessions)
8391158a-d3fa-416c-9e98-ee61a2fb12f1.definition: A mechanism that ensures all subsequent requests from a particular client are routed to the same backend server that handled the client's initial request, crucial for stateful applications.

b6cdef10-a788-440b-ac74-501be6c1af12.title: Round Robin (Load Balancing Strategy)
b6cdef10-a788-440b-ac74-501be6c1af12.definition: A load balancing strategy that sequentially directs requests to each server in turn, offering O(1) decision time but not accounting for individual server load or capacity.

c25d18f8-a57b-4086-bdb4-a6fad8259ce6.title: Weighted Round Robin (Load Balancing Strategy)
c25d18f8-a57b-4086-bdb4-a6fad8259ce6.definition: An extension of Round Robin where servers are assigned a weight based on their processing capacity, receiving a proportional number of requests. It also has an O(1) decision time for selection.

a6ba928c-3eb2-4d00-a149-528dac3deb8f.title: Least Connection (Load Balancing Strategy)
a6ba928c-3eb2-4d00-a149-528dac3deb8f.definition: A load balancing strategy that routes new requests to the server with the fewest active connections, requiring the load balancer to maintain connection state and potentially involving O(N) server scans or O(log N) with optimized data structures like a min-heap to find the minimum.

e77741a8-6bb0-414e-a1ad-279ac063fada.title: IP Hash (Load Balancing Strategy)
e77741a8-6bb0-414e-a1ad-279ac063fada.definition: A load balancing strategy that uses a hash of the client’s source IP address to determine the destination server, ensuring session persistence for a given client. It offers O(1) decision time but can lead to uneven distribution or session loss if a server fails.

e3336e2b-b6ed-4be0-ac06-b8a52298b637.title: Least Response Time / Fastest Response Time (Load Balancing Strategy)
e3336e2b-b6ed-4be0-ac06-b8a52298b637.definition: A dynamic load balancing strategy that directs traffic to the server which has demonstrated the quickest response time in recent health checks or actual request processing, requiring active monitoring.

0407b524-5422-4062-bce8-7f5fa5c8d924.title: Content Switching / URL Hash (Load Balancing Strategy)
0407b524-5422-4062-bce8-7f5fa5c8d924.definition: A Layer 7 (Application Layer) load balancing strategy that inspects the request content, such as URL or HTTP headers, to route requests to specific servers or services. It offers fine-grained control but incurs higher processing overhead compared to Layer 4 strategies.

cdc220e1-3315-4a0f-b48a-85eff09d9ad1.title: Predictive / Dynamic Strategies (Load Balancing)
cdc220e1-3315-4a0f-b48a-85eff09d9ad1.definition: Load balancing strategies that leverage machine learning and real-time metrics (e.g., CPU usage, memory, I/O) to proactively distribute load based on anticipated server capacity and current conditions.

52d68816-3205-4078-9052-a3473383579f.title: Weighted Least Connection (Load Balancing Strategy)
52d68816-3205-4078-9052-a3473383579f.definition: A load balancing strategy that combines the Least Connection method with server weights, considering both the number of active connections and the server's assigned processing capacity.

68036445-fcc5-4d44-ae99-c20f0aa4191d.title: Reliability
68036445-fcc5-4d44-ae99-c20f0aa4191d.definition: A system property referring to its ability to perform its required functions under stated conditions for a specified period of time, consistently and without failure.

7437b94b-6a5d-4b0b-a9b0-948d671be47c.title: Health Checks
7437b94b-6a5d-4b0b-a9b0-948d671be47c.definition: Mechanisms used by load balancers to periodically monitor the status and responsiveness of backend servers, ensuring traffic is only directed to healthy and operational servers.

ca5de690-2d4e-481e-b485-6e378d747044.title: Single Point of Failure
ca5de690-2d4e-481e-b485-6e378d747044.definition: A part of a system that, if it fails, will stop the entire system from working. It represents a critical vulnerability in system design.

f7756f20-4760-425e-b3fc-d891ad67f03a.title: High-Availability Configurations
f7756f20-4760-425e-b3fc-d891ad67f03a.definition: Architectural setups, such as active-passive or active-active pairs, designed to ensure continuous system operation and minimize downtime by providing redundancy and automatic failover for critical components like load balancers.

31f8d79b-fa2d-41b0-9a21-36f218abb9d8.title: Performance Bottleneck
31f8d79b-fa2d-41b0-9a21-36f218abb9d8.definition: A point in a system where the capacity is limited, causing a slowdown or constraint on the overall system's performance.

00b12ec8-9309-4044-894d-6cdd5472621e.title: Layer 7 (Application Layer)
00b12ec8-9309-4044-894d-6cdd5472621e.definition: The highest layer of the OSI model, where application-level protocols and data inspection (e.g., HTTP headers, URLs) occur, enabling content-aware load balancing.

a1996d69-077d-4932-baae-c27e91c7369e.title: Layer 4 (Transport Layer)
a1996d69-077d-4932-baae-c27e91c7369e.definition: A layer of the OSI model responsible for end-to-end communication, typically inspecting IP addresses and ports for routing decisions in load balancing.

e75714d1-85a5-4f08-837c-e62040fa272b.title: Consistent Hashing
e75714d1-85a5-4f08-837c-e62040fa272b.definition: A specialized distributed hashing scheme designed to minimize the number of keys that need to be remapped when nodes (servers) are added to or removed from a distributed system. It operates by mapping both data keys and server nodes onto the same conceptual circular hash space, assigning keys to the first node encountered clockwise from the key's position.

ee957019-8d50-476b-8b1a-06f2a6cbec32.title: Virtual Nodes (vnodes)
ee957019-8d50-476b-8b1a-06f2a6cbec32.definition: Multiple points on a conceptual circular hash ring, where each point represents a single physical server. They are introduced in Consistent Hashing to improve load balancing by distributing the load more evenly and smoothing the impact of node failures or additions.

56a8288b-55b9-4251-b32b-d46311059ce6.title: Traditional Modulo Hashing
56a8288b-55b9-4251-b32b-d46311059ce6.definition: A simple hashing method where a key is assigned to a node by calculating `hash(key) % N_nodes`. This approach necessitates remapping nearly all keys when the number of nodes (`N_nodes`) in a system changes.

2fc3ff50-6c41-4dec-b22b-b3c9035d7e2c.title: Circular Hash Space
2fc3ff50-6c41-4dec-b22b-b3c9035d7e2c.definition: A conceptual space, typically represented as a circular ring (e.g., 0 to 2^32 - 1), onto which both data keys and server nodes are mapped in Consistent Hashing. Key assignment is determined by moving clockwise from the key's position to the first encountered node.

0ea10650-fbcc-4526-85e7-7a63f7b0f2bc.title: Distributed Hashing
0ea10650-fbcc-4526-85e7-7a63f7b0f2bc.definition: A method used in distributed systems to distribute data or keys across multiple interconnected nodes (servers) using a hashing function, aiming for efficient data distribution and retrieval.

ab65213f-73bf-4198-aa59-6908a0975ddc.title: Horizontal Scalability
ab65213f-73bf-4198-aa59-6908a0975ddc.definition: The ability of a system to increase its capacity by adding more machines or nodes to a distributed system, allowing for seamless growth and increased performance without requiring fundamental architectural changes or massive data migrations.

f4b2c6ef-3b13-49a9-b8a6-81510f5dfdc7.title: Aggregate Method
f4b2c6ef-3b13-49a9-b8a6-81510f5dfdc7.definition: A primary method of amortized analysis that calculates the total cost of a sequence of 'n' operations and divides by 'n' to find the amortized cost per operation.

e056d600-4d29-4d61-aaa6-cfcffae4b873.title: Accounting Method
e056d600-4d29-4d61-aaa6-cfcffae4b873.definition: Also known as the banker's method, this amortized analysis technique assigns an amortized cost to each operation, allowing some operations to be 'overcharged' to build up 'credit' for subsequent expensive operations, ensuring the total credit never becomes negative.

3fc2c589-27d1-4830-be37-9c8dd8bbc642.title: Potential Method
3fc2c589-27d1-4830-be37-9c8dd8bbc642.definition: Also known as the physicist's method, this amortized analysis technique defines a potential function for the data structure's state, where the amortized cost of an operation is its actual cost plus the change in the potential function.

0d17c961-487d-44ff-a31f-d7bf2d4d8441.title: Average-case Analysis
0d17c961-487d-44ff-a31f-d7bf2d4d8441.definition: A complexity analysis technique that relies on probabilistic assumptions about input distributions to determine the expected performance of an algorithm, distinct from amortized analysis which provides guarantees over worst-case sequences.

435300e2-e432-4e7b-9e1f-a7faecb2dd95.title: Worst-case Analysis
435300e2-e432-4e7b-9e1f-a7faecb2dd95.definition: A complexity analysis technique that focuses solely on the maximum possible cost of a single operation, without considering the sequence of operations or typical input distributions.

0cff39b7-9794-4f17-bd40-25470f18695d.title: Potential Function
0cff39b7-9794-4f17-bd40-25470f18695d.definition: A function defined for the state of a data structure, used in the potential method of amortized analysis to account for the cost of future operations by capturing the 'potential energy' stored in the data structure.

86ac471f-c459-4648-9b6d-a83ae3277458.title: Dynamic Arrays
86ac471f-c459-4648-9b6d-a83ae3277458.definition: A data structure (like Java's ArrayList or C++'s std::vector) that can grow or shrink in size, achieving an amortized O(1) time complexity for appending elements despite occasional O(N) reallocations when the underlying array needs to be resized.

25be2e47-2b7e-448d-bb89-684976c6ce12.title: Hash Tables
25be2e47-2b7e-448d-bb89-684976c6ce12.definition: A data structure (like Java's HashMap or Python's dict) that uses a hash function to map keys to values, offering amortized O(1) for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations, assuming a good hash function and occasional rehashing.

033bcb94-d028-40cb-9900-b868a8719775.title: Disjoint Set Union (DSU) Data Structure
033bcb94-d028-40cb-9900-b868a8719775.definition: A data structure that manages a collection of disjoint sets, commonly optimized with path compression and union by rank/size to achieve a nearly constant amortized time complexity, often expressed as O(α(N)).

78f56787-46f0-4ca8-8790-d4633fa470c5.title: Deadlock
78f56787-46f0-4ca8-8790-d4633fa470c5.definition: A state in operating systems where two or more processes are blocked indefinitely, each waiting for a resource held by another process in the same set.

fcf8b65a-f039-4f5a-a43f-5e5c07cf3b8b.title: Resource Allocation Graph (RAG)
fcf8b65a-f039-4f5a-a43f-5e5c07cf3b8b.definition: A graphical model used to analyze deadlocks, where nodes represent processes and resource types, and directed edges indicate resource requests or assignments; a cycle in a RAG with single-instance resource types signifies a deadlock.

7fd5eb59-ef44-4cd3-80f8-d0c74ee36696.title: Banker's Algorithm
7fd5eb59-ef44-4cd3-80f8-d0c74ee36696.definition: An algorithm for deadlock avoidance that requires processes to declare maximum resource needs in advance and performs a safety check to ensure resource allocation maintains a safe state, with a time complexity of O(m*n^2).

9969e939-ec48-4d44-af12-258b44590772.title: Coffman conditions
9969e939-ec48-4d44-af12-258b44590772.definition: Four necessary conditions that must simultaneously hold for a deadlock to arise: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

34b6e65c-8b17-4094-a7a8-80249893c7d2.title: Safe state
34b6e65c-8b17-4094-a7a8-80249893c7d2.definition: A state in a system from which all processes can complete without deadlocking, typically in the context of deadlock avoidance.

75408f39-ebad-45c3-9f71-274ec3b012ce.title: Deadlock detection and recovery
75408f39-ebad-45c3-9f71-274ec3b012ce.definition: A strategy for handling deadlocks where the system allows deadlocks to occur, periodically runs a detection algorithm (e.g., graph traversal for cycles), and then recovers by either terminating processes or preempting resources and rolling back process states.

7eab6019-021e-4974-a5c2-48d7f5a137a8.title: Deadlock prevention
7eab6019-021e-4974-a5c2-48d7f5a137a8.definition: A strategy for handling deadlocks that ensures at least one of the four necessary Coffman conditions never occurs (e.g., requiring processes to request all resources at once or imposing a total ordering on resource acquisition).

ec5255b5-891f-499c-96df-63df1d9d83e3.title: Deadlock avoidance
ec5255b5-891f-499c-96df-63df1d9d83e3.definition: A strategy for handling deadlocks that dynamically allocates resources only if doing so leaves the system in a safe state.

cfc665bd-fc13-42be-9556-063a48299663.title: Hold and wait
cfc665bd-fc13-42be-9556-063a48299663.definition: A necessary condition for deadlock, where a process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes.

64c4e588-85c8-4c7b-a2bd-354390c8285d.title: Circular wait
64c4e588-85c8-4c7b-a2bd-354390c8285d.definition: A necessary condition for deadlock, where a set of processes {P0, P1, ..., Pn} exists such that P0 is waiting for a resource held by P1, P1 for P2, and so on, with Pn ultimately waiting for P0.

87b589c2-6a08-488e-9683-f75e88ae2f13.title: Mutual exclusion
87b589c2-6a08-488e-9683-f75e88ae2f13.definition: A necessary condition for deadlock, meaning at least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode.

889bd65f-4248-4cc2-8d2e-50f422b52ba8.title: No preemption
889bd65f-4248-4cc2-8d2e-50f422b52ba8.definition: A necessary condition for deadlock, implying resources cannot be forcibly removed from a process holding them.

c055e84e-8c05-4bd1-ba2c-58e608d8981c.title: Ostrich Algorithm
c055e84e-8c05-4bd1-ba2c-58e608d8981c.definition: An ignorance strategy for handling deadlocks, where the system ignores the problem, relying on deadlocks being rare and the overhead of prevention or avoidance being substantial.

88aeea19-42ee-4f79-b8d2-1f57d696a544.title: Improper lock ordering
88aeea19-42ee-4f79-b8d2-1f57d696a544.definition: A common pitfall leading to deadlocks where locks are acquired in different sequences by different processes, creating conditions for circular wait.

84ddf53f-7f01-4027-8340-677f7d09e8ed.title: Holding locks for excessively long durations
84ddf53f-7f01-4027-8340-677f7d09e8ed.definition: A common pitfall that increases the likelihood of deadlocks by increasing the time window during which other processes might contend for the locked resources, contributing to 'hold and wait'.

b7b3bbee-5d72-41de-8759-08ed19c3768f.title: Mixing incompatible synchronization primitives
b7b3bbee-5d72-41de-8759-08ed19c3768f.definition: A common pitfall that can lead to deadlocks or other concurrency issues due to inconsistent behavior or subtle interactions between different mechanisms not designed to work seamlessly together.

906bbab7-862b-43fb-bcc3-8eed907235c7.title: Negative edge weights
906bbab7-862b-43fb-bcc3-8eed907235c7.definition: A property of a graph edge where the weight (cost) associated with traversing it is a negative value. These can cause issues for some shortest path algorithms, notably Dijkstra's.

40ad0eba-52bb-4ce0-85ff-17e5b90baae9.title: Negative cycles
40ad0eba-52bb-4ce0-85ff-17e5b90baae9.definition: A cycle in a graph where the sum of the weights of its edges is negative. Such cycles imply an infinitely short path, leading to undefined shortest paths, and can be detected by algorithms like Bellman-Ford.

4e577468-6c01-4ee4-9cb8-69ec8994f39c.title: Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP)
4e577468-6c01-4ee4-9cb8-69ec8994f39c.definition: A category of shortest path problems that aims to find the shortest paths from a single designated source node to all other nodes in a graph.

75b11c2e-509f-4005-9fba-d42d26a9316b.title: All-Pairs Shortest Path (APSP)
75b11c2e-509f-4005-9fba-d42d26a9316b.definition: A category of shortest path problems that aims to find the shortest paths between all possible pairs of nodes in a graph.

8f62dc94-93ad-486e-82e5-658b7e33f575.title: Johnson's algorithm
8f62dc94-93ad-486e-82e5-658b7e33f575.definition: An all-pairs shortest path (APSP) algorithm that can handle graphs with negative edge weights by first re-weighting edges (typically using Bellman-Ford) and then running Dijkstra's algorithm V times. It is particularly efficient for sparse graphs.

ad079234-c7f2-4dc8-9fd7-b20ab0769544.title: Shortest Path Problem
ad079234-c7f2-4dc8-9fd7-b20ab0769544.definition: The problem of finding a path between two nodes (or all pairs of nodes) in a graph such that the sum of the weights of its constituent edges is minimized.

e891d80a-7ff6-44fa-b1e9-c8fee98a4c06.title: Transitive closure of a graph
e891d80a-7ff6-44fa-b1e9-c8fee98a4c06.definition: A graph operation that results in a new graph where an edge (u,v) exists if and only if there is a path from u to v in the original graph. Floyd-Warshall algorithm can be used for this application.

c96e66b5-b52c-4e91-a395-d2a109b710e5.title: Memory management
c96e66b5-b52c-4e91-a395-d2a109b710e5.definition: The operating system's crucial function of allocating and deallocating memory resources to running processes, ensuring efficient utilization, protection, and isolation.

4bb49c5b-055e-41bf-963e-41c585e88771.title: Virtual memory
4bb49c5b-055e-41bf-963e-41c585e88771.definition: An abstraction layer over physical RAM that presents each process with a large, contiguous, and private address space, independent of actual physical memory layout or size, achieved primarily through paging.

31e53728-c25e-4516-aef8-b3aa6ac6bb77.title: Page table
31e53728-c25e-4516-aef8-b3aa6ac6bb77.definition: A data structure maintained by the operating system that maps virtual pages to physical frames, used by the MMU for address translation.

46ddf0d5-4eae-4234-b5ed-50cfb49cf808.title: Paging
46ddf0d5-4eae-4234-b5ed-50cfb49cf808.definition: A mechanism within virtual memory where the virtual address space is divided into fixed-size units called pages, and the physical memory into equally sized frames, used for translating virtual addresses to physical addresses.

1ad07902-7454-459a-879d-6cdf201b227d.title: Thrashing
1ad07902-7454-459a-879d-6cdf201b227d.definition: A performance degradation state in a virtual memory system where the system spends an excessive amount of time paging data between RAM and disk due to insufficient physical memory, leading to drastically reduced throughput.

fceb48e6-7dbd-437a-9da3-fe25f876bc1c.title: Page fault
fceb48e6-7dbd-437a-9da3-fe25f876bc1c.definition: An event that occurs when a process attempts to access a virtual page that is not currently resident in physical memory, triggering the operating system to load the page from secondary storage.

14b54cc0-5d51-4ab0-ba82-3b3037a487ed.title: Demand paging
14b54cc0-5d51-4ab0-ba82-3b3037a487ed.definition: A memory management technique, also known as swapping, where pages are loaded into physical memory only when they are referenced (on demand) following a page fault, allowing programs larger than physical RAM to run.

bed2d18c-b270-4b24-98b0-066e72d4cf31.title: Memory Management Unit (MMU)
bed2d18c-b270-4b24-98b0-066e72d4cf31.definition: A hardware component that translates virtual addresses generated by the CPU into physical addresses using a page table.

2e791190-9936-49aa-ab0c-59e77bed2b4a.title: Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)
2e791190-9936-49aa-ab0c-59e77bed2b4a.definition: A small, fast hardware cache that stores recent virtual-to-physical address mappings to accelerate address translation, offering O(1) average access time on a hit.

dfa97491-40c3-4750-8dc8-2d4e3cc2afc1.title: Page replacement algorithms
dfa97491-40c3-4750-8dc8-2d4e3cc2afc1.definition: Algorithms (e.g., LRU, FIFO, Clock) used by the operating system to decide which page to evict from physical memory when a new page needs to be loaded and all frames are occupied.

29ad43d7-4fbe-4485-ab80-0e5a97d89f62.title: Multi-level page tables
29ad43d7-4fbe-4485-ab80-0e5a97d89f62.definition: A hierarchical organization of page tables used by modern operating systems to reduce the physical memory overhead associated with very large virtual address spaces.

dab79467-9da4-49a4-8382-6adaf71f7432.title: Inverted page tables
dab79467-9da4-49a4-8382-6adaf71f7432.definition: A type of page table that stores one entry per physical frame, rather than one per virtual page, aiming to reduce the physical memory overhead, particularly for systems with many processes.

aa40893b-362f-4fa4-a0e3-1c9416b5c224.title: Pages
aa40893b-362f-4fa4-a0e3-1c9416b5c224.definition: Fixed-size units into which the virtual address space is divided in a paging system.

35e68572-0d2a-40cd-b940-0f3c49564e0e.title: Frames
35e68572-0d2a-40cd-b940-0f3c49564e0e.definition: Equally sized units into which physical memory is divided to correspond with pages in a paging system.

d481c3f9-a0ac-4d9a-98d8-3fda869fd7d6.title: TLB hit
d481c3f9-a0ac-4d9a-98d8-3fda869fd7d6.definition: An event where a required virtual-to-physical address mapping is found in the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), allowing for fast address translation.

6e67ac77-e9dd-4006-948d-e8d1c88c4e89.title: Virtual address
6e67ac77-e9dd-4006-948d-e8d1c88c4e89.definition: An address generated by the CPU that refers to a location within a process's virtual address space, requiring translation by the MMU to a physical address.

d41b319e-1719-453e-84ce-4cf52da31394.title: Physical address
d41b319e-1719-453e-84ce-4cf52da31394.definition: An actual address in the physical RAM, which results from the translation of a virtual address by the Memory Management Unit (MMU).

49ac260b-8c0a-45fd-bb49-967a5d82adc8.title: Page table walk
49ac260b-8c0a-45fd-bb49-967a5d82adc8.definition: The process of traversing the page table (which can be O(L) for an L-level page table) to find a virtual-to-physical address mapping when a TLB miss occurs.

33f311c4-88d9-4ee7-87b1-2eec5aff8994.title: Swap space
33f311c4-88d9-4ee7-87b1-2eec5aff8994.definition: A designated area on secondary storage (disk) used by the operating system to store virtual pages that are not currently held in physical memory, used during demand paging.

bc91560c-e377-4b68-aa93-1316d62553d4.title: Memory protection
bc91560c-e377-4b68-aa93-1316d62553d4.definition: A benefit of virtual memory that ensures processes are isolated from each other, preventing one process from accessing or corrupting the memory of another.

073c2e17-cc6b-4a1e-b4c0-fc1a9998befd.title: Memory sharing
073c2e17-cc6b-4a1e-b4c0-fc1a9998befd.definition: A benefit of virtual memory that allows multiple processes to efficiently share the same physical memory regions, often used for shared libraries or inter-process communication.

4fba835c-6a19-4858-a06a-d905ad8fadf3.title: TLB miss
4fba835c-6a19-4858-a06a-d905ad8fadf3.definition: An event where a required virtual-to-physical address mapping is not found in the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), necessitating a slower page table walk.

7f37a785-d642-4ad4-86b4-a86b507bbe4a.title: Memory overcommitment
7f37a785-d642-4ad4-86b4-a86b507bbe4a.definition: A technique enabled by virtual memory that allows the operating system to run programs whose total memory requirements exceed the available physical RAM.

21e8799b-563d-4a16-8748-a3fa14eae1ae.title: Internal fragmentation
21e8799b-563d-4a16-8748-a3fa14eae1ae.definition: Wasted space within a memory block (specifically, within pages in a paging system) where the allocated memory is larger than the actual requested memory.

082a9c93-8e1f-47b7-91e6-44a5f487b254.title: External fragmentation
082a9c93-8e1f-47b7-91e6-44a5f487b254.definition: Wasted space outside allocated memory blocks, where total available memory is sufficient, but it is not contiguous enough to satisfy a new allocation request. This is eliminated at the logical level by paging.
